name: aiml-centric
context: Systems where ML is a first-class citizen requiring deep integration of ML pipelines including feature stores, model registries, training infrastructure, and serving layers. This pattern is for organizations building AI/ML products where data science teams need production-grade MLOps infrastructure.
benefits: First-class support for ML workflows with native feature engineering, training, and serving pipelines
Centralized feature repository enables consistent features across multiple models, reducing duplicate engineering effort from 15% to 64%
Versioning, lineage tracking, and approval workflows provide auditability for regulated environments
Continuous training and deployment (CT/CD) reduces model deployment time from 3-6 weeks to 2-5 days
Monitor model drift, performance degradation, and data quality proactively
tradeoffs: Platform complexity with many interconnected components (feature store, model registry, training pipelines, serving infrastructure) require significant DevOps investment
Steep learning curve with numerous tools and frameworks to master
Compliance requirements, bias detection, and explainability add process overhead
Training infrastructure with GPUs is expensive; cost optimization requires careful planning
Requires both ML expertise and DevOps capabilities, making talent acquisition challenging
use_cases: Multiple ML models in production when an organization runs 5+ ML models requiring shared feature engineering and model lifecycle management
Need for model lineage and governance in regulated industries (finance, healthcare) requiring audit trails from training data to predictions
Continuous model retraining for models that degrade over time and require automated retraining pipelines (daily/weekly)
Data science teams needing self-serve infrastructure for experimentation and deployment
Real-time inference requirements with sub-100ms latency for fraud detection, recommendations, or pricing
avoid_when: Simple rules-based logic sufficient: business logic can be implemented with if-then rules without ML
Single, rarely-changed model: one model that rarely needs updates; manual deployment is acceptable
No regulatory requirements: no compliance mandates for model documentation, audit trails, or bias detection
No data science capability: organization lacks data scientists to leverage ML infrastructure
Stable models with infrequent retraining: models that don't degrade over time; batch scoring monthly or quarterly is sufficient
component_types: Feature Store: Centralized feature repository for training and serving with offline (batch) and online (real-time) stores. Solves training-serving skew by providing consistent feature computation.
Model Registry: Versioned model artifacts with metadata, lineage tracking, and lifecycle stage management. Acts as single source of truth for all production models.
Training Pipeline: Automated ML workflow orchestrating data ingestion → feature extraction → training → evaluation → registration with CI/CD integration.
Model Serving: Infrastructure for real-time and batch inference with monitoring, auto-scaling, and rollback capabilities.
ML Platform: Self-serve infrastructure providing data scientists with experiment tracking, compute resources, and deployment tools.
Experiment Tracking: System for logging training runs, parameters, metrics, and artifacts for reproducibility and comparison.
Model Monitoring: Observability layer tracking model performance, data drift, concept drift, and prediction quality.
Feature Engineering: Transform raw data into numerical features that models consume, with point-in-time correctness for training.
Data Ingestion: Collect and validate data from various sources, ensuring data quality before feature extraction.
Inference Gateway: API layer handling routing, load balancing, and model ensemble for inference requests.
anti_patterns: Monolith ML: single monolithic model codebase where all components are tightly coupled; changes to one model affect others
Not-so-microservices: treating ML services like regular microservices without addressing data/model complexity; leads to distributed monolith
Shared Feature Store Bottleneck: centralized feature store becomes a scaling bottleneck and single point of failure
Training-Serving Skew: inconsistent feature computation between training and inference environments; model accuracy drops in production
Manual Model Deployment: no CI/CD for models; manual deployment leads to inconsistencies and slow iteration
Shadow Puppets: running shadow mode indefinitely without transitioning to full deployment
Feature Engineering Debt: duplicating feature logic across training and serving codebases
design_principles: ML as First-Class Citizen: Design infrastructure where ML components are not afterthoughts but core architectural elements with proper support for the ML lifecycle
Feature Consistency: Use a feature store to ensure identical feature computation for both training and serving, eliminating training-serving skew
Model Governance: Implement version control, lineage tracking, and approval workflows for all models to meet regulatory compliance requirements
Automation First: Automate the entire ML pipeline from data ingestion through training, evaluation, and deployment to enable continuous model improvement
Observability: Monitor model performance, data drift, and concept drift proactively to catch issues before they impact business outcomes
Separation of Concerns: Keep data engineering, data science, and ML engineering concerns distinct with well-defined handoff points
Reproducibility: Version all ML artifacts including data, code, features, and models to enable exact reproduction of any model
best_practices: Feature Store Implementation: Deploy a feature store early to prevent training-serving skew; default to batch features, upgrade to streaming only when latency-sensitive use cases require it
Model Registry Governance: Define mandatory metadata schema for every registered model; enforce approval workflows for production promotion
Pipeline Automation: Build CI/CD pipelines for models that run data validation, training, evaluation, and deployment automatically
Experiment Tracking: Log all training runs with parameters, metrics, and artifacts; enable comparison and reproduction of experiments
Monitoring Strategy: Implement drift detection for data, features, and predictions; set up alerts for degradation thresholds
Cost Optimization: Use auto-scaling for inference endpoints; schedule GPU training during off-peak hours; implement model distillation for cheaper serving
Team Structure: Separate platform teams (building infrastructure) from product teams (consuming infrastructure); enable self-service capabilities
